newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Nordic travel agents boycott SAS over fees.
newsitem.headline: Nordic travel agents boycott SAS over fees.

text.p: Nordic travel agents have launched a boycott of Scandinavian Airlines System (SAS) in retaliation for the airline's decision to cut agents' commissions on domestic and intra-Scandinavian flights.
"This is the start of a war between SAS and the travel agents," said industry consultant Peter Nordstrom from Andersen Consulting.
"(It is also) the first step towards a new market with many options for customers to book tickets through many channels."

The row over Scandinavian skies broke out at the turn of the year after SAS decided to cut travel agents' commissions to five percent from eight percent for domestic flights and to five percent from nine for intra-Scandinavia flights.
"Domestic and intra-Scandinavian ticket booking has become so much easier with IT," said SAS spokesman Peter Forssman, explaining the cut that comes into effect in April.
But travel agents were strongly opposed to the move by SAS which dominates air travel in Scandinavia, owned partly by the governments of Sweden, Denmark and Norway.
Norway's travel agent association said from Monday onwards its employees would present other travel alternatives to clients rather than give out SAS details.
Seven Danish members of the Guild of European Business Travel Agents late last week said that as far as possible they would book customers on rival airlines to SAS.
However the Swedish travel trade federation, that handles 90 percent of the country's travel agent sector, was more cautious.
"We will keep offering our customers the best available alternative which in Sweden often is SAS," Stephan Ekstrom, the federation's chairman, told Reuters.
"But SAS's decision could mean that we might start thinking broader and looking at other alternatives than SAS if they are good for the customer."
Ekstrom said the Swedish association preferred to hold off from implementing any harsh measures until it had negotiated with SAS.
Aviation analysts were not sure SAS will be able to see through the announced cuts.
"SAS could have to back down somewhat in negotiations," Nordstrom said.
SAS, however, is not alone as it eyes travel agents' profits.
Its cooperation partner Lufthansa, Germany's main carrier, also announced in December that it intended to trim travel agents' commissions from May this year.
Lufthansa will cut commissions on domestic German flights to five percent from eight percent, according to Lars Edelgard, head of marketing at Lufthansa in Sweden.
In the U.S., domestic airlines announced similar cuts last spring and analysts think other airlines could follow suit.
"I have talked to several (Swedish) airlines and it seems as if they will follow SAS," analyst Bo Sehlberg, who issues the Swedish newsletter Flygrevyn Express, told Reuters.
"They very much agree that travel agents get too much for their services."
Sehlberg said SAS's proposal could mean travel agents' profits are halved and lead to the closure of some branches.
"A reduction in branch offices would mean a disadvantage for SAS as the competition with (Swedish national railway) SJ would toughen," Sehlberg said.
